stade-rep5a-670-f83-85.summary: A refugee at Bender, on Ottoman soil, since Poltava, Charles XII learns of the rout of the Danish army at Helsingborg. In a chancery letter whose sensitive passages are in cipher, he declares himself ready to make peace with Denmark under the mediation of England and the United Provinces, and gives the Council a “free hand” to negotiate and to conclude an armistice, “even for a whole year”. Two ciphered copies, received by the Swedish government of Bremen-Verden, are kept at Stade.
stade-rep5a-670-f83-85.en: Charles. Since we have lately learnt that the King of Denmark’s army, which last autumn was shipped over into Scania, has a short while ago, in an action, been utterly overcome, beaten and scattered, we may rightly conclude that the said King — inasmuch as the just God has thus punished his faithlessness and his wrongful dealing against his given word and seal — will change his evil designs and willingly seek to come to terms with us.

system: homophonic Swedish nomenclator of about 1,100 numbers in alphabetical order: letters (31–98, two series), syllables (99–182), numbers (183–211), endings (212–304), words and names (310–1102); powers written as sigla in clear: B.B. = Denmark, LL = England, ddd…
